title: CANDIDATE PROFILES: Le Sueur County Commissioners District 4 - NewsBreak
text:
By CARSON HUGHES ,
1 days ago
Ahead of the Aug. 11 primaries, the Le Sueur County News offered candidates running to represent District 4 on the Le Sueur County Board of Commissioners an opportunity to sit down for a face-to-face interview on the issues impacting Le Sueur County today.
We reached out to each of the three candidates running to represent the cities of Le Center, Kilkenny and Waterville as Kilkenny, Cordova and Washington Townships on the Board of Commissioners. Out of the three candidates: Travis Bowman, David Preisler and Tessie Splett, Preisler agreed to the in-person interview. A transcript of that conversation, edited for clarity, length and conciseness is included below.
Name: David Preisler
Age: 62
Home: Le Center
Occupation: Retired 28-year CEO of the Minnesota Pork Producers Association
Past Government Experience: Four years on the Le Sueur County Board of Commissioners
Why are you seeking another term on the county board?
When I first ran, I didn’t run on any single hot button issue — and I don’t think that changes this time around either. There are a lot of things that we’ve done successfully over the last, almost four years now from a standpoint of completely redone all of our financial policies, board operating procedures, established a ditch manual and now we’re actively rewriting all of our ordinances. The ordinance piece is really to make development more transparent, easier to understand and also is much closer to the standards that are in our neighboring counties and to reduce regulation while still avoiding conflicting uses. We’ll have that done yet this year, but I think we’ve accomplished a lot and look forward into the future to continue to problem solve, continue to listen to people and continue to make Le Sueur County the best place that it can be.
Where do you see some of the biggest issues in the county code that need to be addressed?
From a standpoint of having work sessions on that, and that won’t be finished until probably December when we’ll have the final package that will be ready to be acted on, and also there will be public hearings on all of those before that occurs. We just have got in a lot of different places we go above and beyond, for example, some things that the DNR has for regulation in shorelands and I think that there’s some areas where we may have actually gone a little too far. So we need to analyze the why of that and again, try and get things to where they’re more understandable and more workable for homeowners and contractors.
Do you see any particular changes you would like to make to permitting processes?
Yeah, I think that there are some processes that we can move to. More over the counter permits. Instead of having a number of those things go to our planning and zoning commission. Really, our planning and zoning commission should be for those kinds of developments that are really different, something we maybe haven’t seen very much of before then, to wrestle through kind of policy issues on that. But if we’ve got a type of activity that we’ve seen a number of different times and, we’re regulating it in a very consistent way, that should be able to be done within a permit over the counter, rather than going through the time and the expense of a conditional use process. And so we’re reviewing that in all of the ordinances. It should result in more timely and more cost effective permitting.
Many comments that came up during the Comprehensive Plan hearings are from people wanting to keep that agricultural nature of Le Sueur County. Where do you see the balance in that, as well as setting up Le Sueur county for further growth?
I think the vast majority of folks don’t want to lose that rural character and I agree with that. But that’s where, you know, thoughtful discussion in the ordinance revisions is going to help guide us there. Again, I think most of the job creating growth is probably going to take place within cities because they’re the ones that have got areas identified for commercial industrial development and I don’t see those things as mutually exclusive. I think that we can maintain a rural character and yet grow job opportunities.
We recently saw a moratorium on data centers in Le Sueur County for the next year. Going beyond that moratorium, do you see potential room for a data center being built in Le Sueur County?
First of all, I’m the one that made the motion to do the moratorium and really because we don’t have anything in our existing ordinances that address data centers. So what a moratorium gives you is it gives you time to logically work through that whole discussion. My personal belief is that data centers belong in commercial industrial zoned areas, not on agricultural land, but we need to take this time now to study, learn from others and also see what happens with technology changes.
I have no interest in this first generation of data centers with their power requirements and their water requirements, but there are newer technologies that recycle all the water that I think, just like any business, technology changes and so to say automatically, no, never, forever, probably isn’t the appropriate answer.
What would you say are the biggest challenges facing Le Sueur County?
I think there’s a couple of things. One is financial, and that is some of the cost shifts and mandates that have come from both the federal and the state government. So, for example, we are mandated to provide the service, and yet the state or federal government either shifts more of the financial responsibility to the county or all of the financial responsibility to the county. We can’t not provide the service because it’s mandated by law, yet the shifts of costs or just an outright mandate where they make us absorb all the costs are a big wild card in financial planning for the county.
I think that’s where I bring a different skillset than what you’d see in most commissioners, is that I do have years of professional experience lobbying the legislature successfully to make changes. And I spend time lobbying and also testifying on bills at the state legislature this past year to push against those cost shifts.
I think the other thing is the inflationary kind of place where all businesses are at today and all homes are at today from just cost pressures going up. As we have more expensive fuel, that affects what the cost is to plow a road or to rebuild a road. As you have more expensive parts and more expensive technology, that affects what happens in our Sheriff’s Department’s budget, in road and bridge, in lots of different budgets.
How do you see the county maintaining the level of service that it does provide with these financial pressures?
I think that ends up being the ultimate challenge, and I think that’s why it’s really important to be engaged wwith the federal government and the state government, because about half of our county’s budget comes from either the federal government or the state government. Really we’re the delivery mechanism for services that both those levels of government have mandated. We need to be at the table with both the federal and state government to push against the mandates that aren’t funded or the shifts that have recurring costs of services
Where do you see the county having room to improve its services when those costs do come down from higher up?
As we go through our budgeting process, we literally go through every line item in the budget with every department. We’ve also told them that oftentimes there is this behavior that happens no matter what business you’re in. You get to the end of the year, and if you’ve got some extra money left over, they may spend it so they don’t lose it next year. That is not how we manage here. We want to judge each budget year on its own merits, and I think you have to get into that sort of detail and discussion in order to identify places for efficiencies if they can happen, and just improve processes wherever we can.
I think the other thing is that we are in a position where we have no need to take on additional debt or do bonding. So if you’re not borrowing money and instead you’re paying debt off, it starts to give you some more room then within the budget to help absorb some of these inflationary pressures and I think that’s an important thing to keep in mind that we don’t have a need to do that within the next five years. At least, it doesn’t appear within the plan and I don’t see it happening.

The ordinance piece is really to make development more transparent, easier to understand and also is much closer to the standards that are in our neighboring counties and to reduce regulation while still avoiding conflicting uses.
